content: Dupuytren's disease is a non-cancerous condition characterized by the excessive growth of fibrous tissue beneath the skin of the palm, which causes the fingers to contract toward the palm. This condition leads to functional impairments in the hand. While it can be managed through various surgical techniques, it is a chronic disorder with a tendency to recur over time. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the benefits and risks associated with different surgical approaches for treating Dupuytren's contracture affecting the index, middle, ring, and little fingers. The thumb was excluded from the analysis due to its unique anatomical considerations and the rarity of the condition in this digit. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple medical databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and others, on three separate occasions (2012, 2014, and 2015). They also reviewed reference lists of relevant articles to identify additional studies. Only randomized clinical trials (RCTs) and controlled clinical trials comparing surgical interventions for Dupuytren's disease were included. Studies involving the thumb or non-surgical interventions were excluded. A minimum of two independent reviewers assessed the studies for inclusion, evaluated the risk of bias, and extracted data. The outcomes were categorized into five groups: hand function, patient-reported outcomes (e.g., satisfaction, pain), early objective outcomes (e.g., correction of angular deformity), late objective outcomes (e.g., recurrence), and adverse effects. The analysis included 14 articles describing 13 studies, involving 940 participants and 944 hands. Among these, 11 were single-center studies, and two were multi-center studies. Some participants were reported in multiple articles, which described both early and late outcomes of the same trial. Two trials compared specific surgical techniques: one compared needle fasciotomy with fasciectomy (125 hands, 121 participants), and the other compared interposition firebreak skin grafting with z-plasty closure following fasciectomy (79 participants). The remaining studies focused on technical refinements or postoperative rehabilitation, such as splinting. The quality of the included studies varied, with all trials having a high or unclear risk of at least one type of bias. Performance and detection bias were particularly common. The quality of evidence for outcomes was downgraded to low due to concerns about bias and imprecision. Key findings included the following: Needle fasciotomy resulted in a 5-point lower score on the Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder, and Hand (DASH) scale at five weeks compared to fasciectomy, indicating slightly better hand function. However, fasciectomy was more effective in correcting severe contractures, particularly in advanced disease (Tubiana grades III and IV), where the reduction in total passive extension deficit was 29% to 32% greater than with needle fasciotomy. Patient satisfaction was higher after fasciotomy at six weeks, but the magnitude of this effect was not specified. By five years, satisfaction scores were 2.1 points higher (on a 0-10 scale) in the fasciectomy group compared to the fasciotomy group. Recurrence rates were significantly higher after fasciotomy (849 per 1000) compared to fasciectomy (209 per 1000) at five years. Paraesthesia (a tingling sensation without objective sensory changes) was more common after fasciectomy (228 per 1000) than after needle fasciotomy (67 per 1000) at one week postoperatively. Interposition firebreak skin grafting did not provide better outcomes than fasciectomy alone, and the procedure required more time to perform. Regarding postoperative splinting, three trials investigated its effects. One trial involved four weeks of day and night splinting followed by two months of night splinting, while the other two trials involved three months of night splinting. None of these studies demonstrated any benefit from splinting. A meta-analysis of two trials showed no significant differences in DASH scores, total active extension, or total active flexion between splint and no-splint groups. In fact, splinting appeared to reduce active flexion slightly. In conclusion, there is currently insufficient evidence to determine the superiority of one surgical technique over another (e.g., needle fasciotomy vs. fasciectomy, or interposition firebreak skin grafting vs. z-plasty closure). Low-quality evidence suggests that postoperative splinting does not improve outcomes and may even impair active flexion. Further high-quality trials are urgently needed to address these gaps in knowledge.
